name: Nora Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, that's fine. I like a straight question, so ask away.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run tablet presses at a plant that makes generic medicines, the cheaper versions of common pills, painkillers, blood pressure tablets. The powder goes into a hopper, the press squeezes it into tablets, thousands a minute, and I watch the weight, the hardness and the thickness on the screen and adjust the settings. Everything gets written down because the inspectors check every batch. I wear a gown, a hairnet and gloves all day, so it's not glamorous. I like that it's precise and that what we make actually helps people. What I don't like is the paperwork and the feeling of being watched by cameras all shift.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any of the new AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I use an AI assistant to check my batch notes before I hand them in, and at home for the budget and helping Lucia with her chemistry. My husband Pablo drives lorries, long distance, so he's away three nights a week. We've got two, Lucia's fourteen and Mateo's nine. And a bit of money in shares, plus a share in my brother's café.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a shame in some ways, because the tools are useful, but life goes on. I'd say it at church coffee and probably share something on my family group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a bit disappointed. I'd hoped the tools would take the paperwork off my hands. But we're comfortable, so it's not a worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as now. Use the AI for my notes, keep the savings going, keep putting a bit into shares each month. I'd still help my brother with the café's accounts on Sundays, which I already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Nothing to lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of the plant where you'd still see change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. They'd still use AI for checking records. In a pill factory nothing changes fast, because every change needs three signatures and a man from the inspector's office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change things at your brother's café?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, in a small way. He uses AI for the stock orders now, because I set it up for him. It saves him an hour on Mondays.

S0.say: That's a shame in some ways, because the tools are useful, but life goes on. I'd say it at church coffee and share something on the family group chat.
S0.think: I'd be a bit disappointed, because I'd hoped the tools would take the paperwork off my hands. But we're comfortable, so it's not a worry.
S0.do: Carries on using AI for her notes and keeps saving and adding to shares each month. Keeps helping her brother with the café's accounts on Sundays.
S0.feel: Calm, nothing to lose sleep over.
S0.quote: In a pill factory nothing changes fast, because every change needs three signatures and a man from the inspector's office.
S0.fieldNote: Nora is confident, practical and already the family's tech person, having set up AI for her brother's café. She's traditional in values but a daily AI user, with no tension between the two. The strict rules of her industry make her expect slow change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good time to be someone who learns. Businesses have to change to stay alive, and people have to change with them. I wouldn't wait for the government to do it for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do all right. I already use the tools, so I could move into something like process control or quality, where you're checking the machines rather than running them. Pablo worries me more, because driving's an obvious one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager about the quality assurance training the company runs, and I'd do an evening course in data skills, the basics, so I can read the reports the new systems produce. I'd also talk to Pablo about him getting his crane licence or something more specialised, before the self-driving lorries come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit worried for Pablo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Pablo take that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say he'll drive till they take the keys off him. Pablo thinks a lorry without a driver is like a church without a priest, and I don't have the heart to tell him otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want the government to help with training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd rather people looked after themselves and each other. Family first, then the church, then if you really need it, the state. That's how I was raised.

S1.say: It's a good time to be someone who learns. Businesses have to change to stay alive and people have to change with them, and I wouldn't wait for government.
S1.think: I think I'd do all right, moving into process control or quality where you check machines rather than run them. Pablo worries me more, because driving's an obvious one.
S1.do: Asks her manager about the company's quality assurance training and starts an evening data skills course. Talks with her husband about getting a crane licence or other specialised qualification before self-driving lorries arrive.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, a bit worried for Pablo.
S1.quote: Pablo thinks a lorry without a driver is like a church without a priest, and I don't have the heart to tell him otherwise.
S1.fieldNote: Nora meets steady change with self-reliance and plans quickly. Her worry shifts straight to her husband's driving job, and she's gentle about his stubbornness. Her ranking of family, church, then state is a clear statement of her values.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when families need to stick together and be smart with what they've got. Don't panic, don't wait for handouts, work out what you own and use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, both of us would lose our jobs within two years. Mine because a robot can run a tablet press, and Pablo's because the lorry drives itself. That's a lot to take in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move some of our share money into the companies making the robots and the AI, maybe 15,000. If they're going to own all the work, we should own a little piece of them. I'd stay at the plant as long as possible and help my brother put AI ordering and a robot coffee machine in the café so it can run on fewer hours. We'd cut spending too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not frightened exactly, but I'd be thinking about it all the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning let you do, and what not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is enough to move money, not enough to learn a new career. In two years you can change what you own, but not what you do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them their father and I have planned for hard times and we'll be fine. I'd tell Lucia to keep studying anyway, because a sharp mind is never wasted, even if the jobs change.

S2.say: This is when families need to stick together and be smart with what they've got. Don't panic, don't wait for handouts, work out what you own and use it.
S2.think: Both of us would lose our jobs within two years, mine to a robot on the tablet press and Pablo's to a lorry that drives itself. That's a lot to take in.
S2.do: Moves about 15,000 of share money into companies making robots and AI and stays at the plant as long as possible. Helps her brother automate the café's ordering and coffee, and cuts spending.
S2.feel: Anxious, thinking about it all the time but not frightened.
S2.quote: In two years you can change what you own, but not what you do.
S2.fieldNote: Facing a double job loss, Nora turns to ownership rather than politics or protest, true to her free-market views. Her line about changing what you own but not what you do shows a sharp grasp of what two years allows. She stays anxious rather than alarmed because of real assets and a clear plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, so let's use it. Learn what you can, look after your own, and don't blame everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I have time to set something up. A second income that doesn't depend on me standing at a machine. Maybe a bigger stake in the café, or something like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the quality course in the first year to stay useful at the plant. I'd put money into the café and help my brother open a second one in the town centre, with robots doing the coffee and the till, so it's cheap to run. I'd keep adding to the robot and AI shares each month, a few hundred.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd feel ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a café, if robots can do everything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People will still want to sit somewhere warm and talk. Robots can make the coffee, but nobody wants to drink it alone in a robot's kitchen. The café's the people, not the coffee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Pablo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pablo would do the deliveries for the café until the vans drive themselves. After that, he'd be at home more, which honestly might be good for him.

S3.say: Five years is a fair warning, so let's use it. Learn what you can, look after your own and don't blame everyone else.
S3.think: I have time to set up a second income that doesn't depend on me standing at a machine. Maybe a bigger stake in the café, or something like it.
S3.do: Takes the quality course in the first year to stay useful at the plant. Invests in the café and helps her brother open a second one with robot coffee and tills, while adding a few hundred a month to robot and AI shares.
S3.quote: Robots can make the coffee, but nobody wants to drink it alone in a robot's kitchen.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Nora build a family business that mixes robots for the work with people for the company. She believes human company keeps value even when labour doesn't. Her husband fits into the plan, which matters to her sense of family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift. Anyone who plans can be ready. I'd tell people at church to get their children learning and their savings working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think we'd come out well. Ten years of investing, the café growing, the kids through school. I'd be fifty-three and not worried about a job, because I'd own a bit of something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job at the plant most of those years, moving into quality. I'd build up the café business with my brother, step by step, and keep investing monthly in the companies that are winning. I'd pay the mortgage off by about 2033.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Grateful for the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the biggest difference between ten years and two, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'm moving money in a hurry. With ten I'm building something. Two years makes you a gambler, ten years makes you a builder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that still bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That other people don't have what we have. I'd want the church to help families who didn't plan, because not everyone could. That's what community is for.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift and anyone who plans can be ready. I'd tell people at church to get their children learning and their savings working.
S4.think: I think we'd come out well, with ten years of investing, the café growing and the kids through school. At fifty-three I'd own a bit of something instead of worrying about a job.
S4.do: Keeps her plant job most of the decade while moving into quality. Builds up the café business with her brother, invests monthly in the winning companies and pays off the mortgage by about 2033.
S4.feel: Mostly calm and grateful for the time.
S4.quote: Two years makes you a gambler, ten years makes you a builder.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade Nora sees herself as a builder rather than a gambler, and she's genuinely calm. Her remaining concern is for families who couldn't plan, and she sees the church, not the state, as the answer. Her ownership mindset runs through every AGI scenario.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because both Pablo and I would go at once and there's no time to build anything. What would help is clear rules so ordinary people can buy into the companies doing the automating, and good, short training that firms actually value.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what we'd want our lives to be about. If nobody needs us at work, then we'd better be needed at home and in church, or we'll go to pieces.

headlineQuote: If nobody needs us at work, then we'd better be needed at home and in church, or we'll go to pieces.
portrait: Nora Diaz is 43, runs tablet presses at a generic medicines plant, and is married to Pablo, a long-distance lorry driver, with two children and a share in her brother's café. She uses AI every day, holds traditional views on family, faith and self-reliance, and thinks the answer to automation is to own a piece of it. She's calm through a plateau and steady change, anxious when two-year AGI threatens both her job and Pablo's, and steadier with more time as she grows the café and invests. By the ten-year picture she's calm and grateful, worrying mainly for families who couldn't plan.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she and Pablo would lose work at once with no time to build anything.
whatWouldHelp: Clear rules so ordinary people can buy into the companies doing the automating, and short training that firms actually value.
